intro.why: Every realistic RL problem (images, continuous control, games) has too many states for a table. Function approximation is what turns tabular RL into deep RL, and it brings new failure modes that explain the design of DQN.

sections.title: Why lookup tables fail
sections.plain: Too many states to store or visit; a table learns nothing about states it hasn't seen.
sections.body:
Tabular methods keep one entry per state. Real problems have far too many: a Pacman board, a camera image or a continuous position have astronomically (or infinitely) many states. Most will never be visited even once, and a table says nothing about a state it has not seen.

We need generalisation: learning that one board position is bad should say something about the nearly identical position next to it. Instead of memorising values, we learn a rule ("being cornered by a ghost is bad") that transfers. Function approximation is exactly supervised learning's job, applied to value estimation with targets that come from RL.

sections.title: Parameterised and linear value functions
sections.plain: Describe states by features and compute value as a weighted sum.
sections.body:
Replace the table with $\hat v(s,\mathbf w) \approx v_\pi(s)$, where $\mathbf w \in \mathbb R^d$ and $d \ll |\mathcal S|$. With a feature vector $\mathbf x(s) = [x_1(s), \dots, x_d(s)]^\top$, the linear approximator is

$$\hat v(s,\mathbf w) = \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x(s) = \sum_{i=1}^d w_i\,x_i(s)$$

Updating $\mathbf w$ from one state changes the estimate of every state sharing those features: generalisation for free. The price: with fewer weights than states, values can't all be exact, so we need to decide which errors matter most. The objective weights each state by how often it is visited under the policy, $\mu(s)$:

$$\overline{\text{VE}}(\mathbf w) = \sum_s \mu(s)\big[v_\pi(s) - \hat v(s,\mathbf w)\big]^2$$

sections.title: Stochastic gradient descent on value error
sections.plain: Move the weights a little in the direction that reduces the error on the current sample.
sections.body:
Stochastic gradient descent on one sample with target $U_t$:

$$\mathbf w_{t+1} = \mathbf w_t + \alpha\big[U_t - \hat v(S_t,\mathbf w_t)\big]\nabla\hat v(S_t,\mathbf w_t)$$

For a linear approximator $\nabla \hat v(s,\mathbf w) = \mathbf x(s)$, so the update is simply $\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w + \alpha\,\delta\,\mathbf x(s)$. If $U_t$ is an unbiased estimate of $v_\pi(S_t)$ and α decreases appropriately, $\mathbf w$ converges to a local optimum of $\overline{\text{VE}}$ (the global one for linear).

State aggregation is the simplest linear case: group states, one weight per group, $\mathbf x(s)$ a one-hot group indicator. On a 1,000-state random walk with 10 groups, the estimate is a staircase (ex1).

sections.title: Gradient Monte Carlo vs semi-gradient TD
sections.plain: Use the real return (true gradient) or a bootstrapped target (semi-gradient, faster but biased).
sections.body:
Gradient MC: $U_t = G_t$, an unbiased sample of $v_\pi(S_t)$, so this is true SGD and converges to a local minimum of $\overline{\text{VE}}$.

Semi-gradient TD(0): $U_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\hat v(S_{t+1},\mathbf w)$. The target depends on $\mathbf w$, but we take the gradient only of the estimate, ignoring the target's dependence: hence semi-gradient. It is not true gradient descent, yet it learns faster, works online and in continuing tasks. With linear features and on-policy data it converges to the TD fixed point $\mathbf w_{TD}$, whose error is bounded: $\overline{\text{VE}}(\mathbf w_{TD}) \le \frac{1}{1-\gamma}\min_{\mathbf w}\overline{\text{VE}}(\mathbf w)$.

Worked. $\mathbf x(s) = [1,2]$, $\mathbf x(s') = [0,1]$, $\mathbf w = [0.5, 0.1]$, $r = 1$, $\gamma = 0.9$, $\alpha = 0.1$: $\hat v(s) = 0.70$, $\hat v(s') = 0.10$, target $1.09$, $\delta = 0.39$, $\mathbf w \leftarrow [0.5,0.1] + 0.1\cdot0.39\cdot[1,2] = [0.539, 0.178]$. Both weights move, so every other state using these features changes too.

In ex1 (1,000-state walk) TD's staircase is flatter at the ends than MC's (−0.70/0.71 vs −0.85/0.81 at the extremes, true ≈ ±0.85): the bias of bootstrapping through aggregated neighbours.

sections.title: Feature construction: coarse, tile and RBF coding
sections.plain: Turn a continuous state into many simple overlapping features so nearby states share weights.
sections.body:
• Polynomials of state variables: global features; a cubic in ex2 cannot fit a sine-like value function (RMS error 0.40).
  • Coarse coding: overlapping receptive fields (circles) over the state space; a feature is 1 if the state lies inside its circle. Training one state updates all circles covering it, so nearby states generalise. Large fields generalise broadly; the final resolution depends on the total number of features.
  • Tile coding: several offset grids (tilings); each state activates exactly one tile per tiling. The number of active features is constant, so step sizes are easy to set (α/number of tilings). Efficient and widely used. In ex2, 8 tilings × 10 tiles (88 weights) reach RMS error 0.028.
  • Radial basis functions: like coarse coding with graded membership $x_i(s) = \exp(-\|s - c_i\|^2/2\sigma_i^2)$; smooth, differentiable approximations (12 RBFs: RMS 0.020 in ex2).

Hand-designed features need domain knowledge, and most of a combinatorial set of candidate features turns out useless: a needle in a haystack. That is why deep networks, which learn their own features, took over.

sections.title: Neural approximators and the deadly triad
sections.plain: Networks learn features, but combining approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data can make learning blow up.
sections.body:
Generalisation: a table generalises not at all; coarse/tile coding generalise locally; a neural network generalises globally by learning its own features. The semi-gradient update applies unchanged with $\nabla\hat v$ computed by backpropagation.

Generalisation cuts both ways: an update for one state changes others, sometimes for the worse. The deadly triad is the combination of

  1. function approximation,
  2. bootstrapping (TD or DP targets), and
  3. off-policy training,

which together can make estimates diverge even in tiny problems. Baird's counterexample (7 states, linear features, all rewards 0) diverges under off-policy semi-gradient TD: in ex2 the weight norm grows from 10 to 437 in 1,000 sweeps although the true values are all 0. Any two of the three are generally fine (e.g. linear on-policy TD converges). DQN (M10) is essentially a set of tricks (replay, target networks) to live with the triad.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Non-stationary targets. Unlike supervised learning, RL targets change as the policy and value estimates change, so approximators must cope with moving targets.
  • Gradient-TD methods (GTD, TDC) minimise a projected Bellman error with true gradients and are stable off-policy with linear features.
  • Feature scaling matters for SGD exactly as in supervised learning; unnormalised features make one step size wrong for all.
  • Least-squares TD solves for the linear TD fixed point directly in O(d²) per step: data-efficient when d is moderate.

code.title: State aggregation on the 1,000-state random walk
code.explain: Computes the true values by iterative evaluation, then learns 10 group weights with gradient MC and with semi-gradient TD(0) over 5,000 episodes; finally reproduces the worked update [0.539, 0.178].
mistakes: Forgetting that the gradient of a one-hot feature is the indicator.
Using the MC step size for TD (they need different α).
code.notes: Both RMS errors (~0.13) are dominated by the staircase representation; TD's ends are flatter.
code.code:
"""Gradient Monte Carlo vs semi-gradient TD(0) with state aggregation on a 1000-state random walk.

States 1..1000, start at 500. Each step jumps uniformly 1..100 states left or right; jumping
past either end terminates with reward -1 (left) or +1 (right). gamma = 1.
Features: 10 groups of 100 states (one-hot group indicator), so v_hat(s) = w[group(s)].
"""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, G = 1000, 10
def episode():
    s, traj = 500, []
    while True:
        s2 = s + int(rng.integers(1, 101)) * (1 if rng.random() < 0.5 else -1)
        if s2 < 1: traj.append((s, -1.0, None)); return traj
        if s2 > N: traj.append((s, 1.0, None)); return traj
        traj.append((s, 0.0, s2)); s = s2
grp = lambda s: (s - 1) // 100

# true values by iterative policy evaluation
V = np.zeros(N + 2)
for _ in range(200):
    for s in range(1, N + 1):
        tot = 0.0
        for d in range(1, 101):
            for s2 in (s - d, s + d):
                tot += (-1 if s2 < 1 else 1 if s2 > N else V[s2]) / 200
        V[s] = tot
true = V[1:N + 1]

def learn(method, alpha, episodes=5000):
    w = np.zeros(G)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        traj = episode()
        if method == "MC":
            Gret = traj[-1][1]
            for s, _, _ in traj: w[grp(s)] += alpha * (Gret - w[grp(s)])     # gradient of v_hat wrt w = one-hot
        else:
            for s, r, s2 in traj:
                target = r + (w[grp(s2)] if s2 is not None else 0.0)
                w[grp(s)] += alpha * (target - w[grp(s)])                    # semi-gradient
    return w
for m, a in (("MC", 2e-5 * 100), ("TD", 2e-4 * 10)):
    w = learn(m, a)
    est = w[[grp(s) for s in range(1, N + 1)]]
    print(f"{m}: group values {np.round(w, 2)}  RMS error vs true {np.sqrt(((est - true) ** 2).mean()):.3f}")
print("true values at s = 50, 500, 950:", np.round(true[[49, 499, 949]], 3))

# the worked semi-gradient TD(0) update
x, x2, w, r, g, a = np.array([1, 2.]), np.array([0, 1.]), np.array([.5, .1]), 1, .9, .1
v, v2 = w @ x, w @ x2; delta = r + g * v2 - v
print(f"\nworked: v(s)={v:.2f}, v(s')={v2:.2f}, target={r + g * v2:.2f}, delta={delta:.2f}, w -> {np.round(w + a * delta * x, 3)}")

code.title: Features compared, and Baird's counterexample
code.explain: Fits a sine-plus-slope function from noisy samples with tile coding, RBFs and a cubic polynomial; then runs expected off-policy semi-gradient TD on Baird's 7-state problem and watches the weights diverge.
mistakes: Not dividing α by the number of tilings.
Assuming divergence needs a bug: here it follows from the triad.
code.notes: Tile coding and RBFs fit well with local generalisation; global polynomials don't.
code.code:
"""Feature construction (tile coding vs RBF vs a few polynomials) and the deadly triad (Baird's counterexample)."""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
f = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x) + 0.5 * x            # a 'value function' over x in [0, 1]

def tiles(x, n_tilings=8, n_tiles=10):
    idx = []
    for t in range(n_tilings):
        off = t / (n_tilings * n_tiles)
        idx.append(t * (n_tiles + 1) + int((x + off) * n_tiles))
    v = np.zeros(n_tilings * (n_tiles + 1)); v[idx] = 1; return v
def rbf(x, k=12, width=0.08):
    c = np.linspace(0, 1, k); return np.exp(-(x - c) ** 2 / (2 * width ** 2))
def poly(x, d=3): return np.array([x ** i for i in range(d + 1)])

for name, phi, alpha in (("tile coding (8 tilings x 10)", tiles, 0.1 / 8), ("RBF (12 centres)", rbf, 0.05), ("cubic polynomial", poly, 0.05)):
    w = np.zeros(len(phi(0.5)))
    for _ in range(20000):
        x = rng.random(); feat = phi(x)
        w += alpha * (f(x) + rng.normal(0, 0.1) - w @ feat) * feat     # SGD on noisy targets
    xs = np.linspace(0, 0.999, 200)
    rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean([(w @ phi(x) - f(x)) ** 2 for x in xs]))
    print(f"{name:<30} {len(w):3d} weights, RMS error {rmse:.3f}")

# Baird's counterexample: 7 states, linear features, off-policy semi-gradient TD with all rewards 0 (true v = 0)
X = np.zeros((7, 8))
for i in range(6): X[i, i] = 2; X[i, 7] = 1
X[6, 6] = 1; X[6, 7] = 2
w = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 10, 1.]); gamma, alpha = 0.99, 0.01
for sweep in range(1, 1001):
    # expected semi-gradient TD update under the uniform state distribution of the behaviour policy,
    # with the target policy always taking 'solid' (to state 7): importance ratio 1/(1/7) on solid, 0 on dashed
    upd = np.zeros(8)
    for s in range(7):
        delta = 0 + gamma * X[6] @ w - X[s] @ w
        upd += (1 / 7) * delta * X[s]
    w += alpha * upd
    if sweep in (1, 10, 100, 1000): print(f"Baird sweep {sweep:>4}: |w| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3e}")
print("True values are all 0, yet the weights diverge: approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy.")
